--- title: "ASM Chapter 7" author: "Dr Alun ap Rhisiart" date: "2026-11-02" categories: [code, julia, statistics, asm, ecology] execute: echo: true warning: false output: true engine: julia --- # ASM Chapter 7 ## 7.2 Fixed-Effects Models Chapter 7 of Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists by Kéry and Kellner focuses on fixed-effects and random-effects models, providing practical examples and guidance for ecological data analysis for one-way ANOVA. Like the last chapter, this features two models, and we will translate each into Julia. ### 7.2.1 Generating the data As in previous chapters, we drop into R to generate the data so that it matches the examples in the book. However, first, I want to see how it would be done in Julia. The simulated data here represent snout-to-vent (SVL) lengths of 10 smooth snakes from each of five populations. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Random, Distributions, DataFrames, Statistics, CategoricalArrays Random.seed!(72) nPops = 5 nSample = 10 pop_means = [50, 40, 45, 55, 60] σ = 5 n = nPops * nSample ε = rand(Normal(0, σ), n) pop = repeat(1:5, inner=nSample) means = repeat(pop_means, inner=nSample) X = hcat([pop .== i for i in 1:5]...) # This generates a design matrix encoded efficiently as a bit-matrix y = X * pop_means .+ ε ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 50-element Vector{Float64}: 52.27595066289548 50.910128150562876 50.72039409315752 48.74314029094526 52.73841423960742 48.220327771781236 41.082718975741834 58.62814329350371 49.64865438030759 46.05869170909287 ⋮ 60.48001527570767 59.4134099131295 58.40189626316865 54.358249830477675 63.49871501127612 60.2926800202463 55.73394840533504 70.34854639036769 56.50274401923437 ``` ::: ::: Now let's generate the data in R to match the book's example. Note in this case that 'pop' is treated as a factor (strings), but Turing needs integers, and nSample gets returned as a float, but we need an integer. So I use the values created above instead of `rget` the data from R. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using RCall, DataFrames R""" set.seed(72) nPops <- 5 nSample <- 10 pop.means <- c(50, 40, 45, 55, 60) sigma <- 5 n <- nPops * nSample eps <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma) pop <- factor(rep(1:5, rep(nSample, nPops))) means <- rep(pop.means, rep(nSample, nPops)) X <- as.matrix(model.matrix(~ pop - 1)) y <- as.numeric(X %*% as.matrix(pop.means) + eps) """ @rget y ``` ::: ### 7.2.2 Likelihood analysis The book shows the code for effects parameterization, but the output for means only. In R pop is a factor. We need to use CategoricalArrays.jl in Julia to handle it similarly. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Distributions, GLM, DataFramesMeta # means parameterisation df = DataFrame(y=y, pop=categorical(pop)) model = lm(@formula(y ~ -1 + pop), df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{LinearModel{GLM.LmResp{Vector{Float64}}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} y ~ 0 + pop Coefficients: ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. Std. Error t Pr(>|t|) Lower 95% Upper 95% ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── pop: 1 52.4731 1.35859 38.62 <1e-35 49.7368 55.2095 pop: 2 39.3056 1.35859 28.93 <1e-29 36.5692 42.0419 pop: 3 47.0335 1.35859 34.62 <1e-33 44.2972 49.7699 pop: 4 50.611 1.35859 37.25 <1e-34 47.8747 53.3473 pop: 5 62.2568 1.35859 45.82 <1e-38 59.5205 64.9931 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ``` ::: ::: ### 7.2.5 Bayesian analysis with Turing Heretofore I have not used loops for the likelihood, as it is generally not necessary. In this case I show that you can translate the R code in a way that mirrors the R code more closely. In general you don't need to do this, but if you plan to use predict() later (eg for a Prior Predictive Check), then that function can struggle with vectorised likelihoods. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Turing @model function fixed_effects(y, pop, nPops) # Parameters and Priors alpha ~ filldist(Normal(0, 100), nPops) sigma ~ truncated(Cauchy(0, 10), 0, Inf) # Likelihood: Use a for loop to allow predict() to simulate missing data for i in eachindex(y) y[i] ~ Normal(alpha[pop[i]], sigma) end # Generated Quantities effe2 = alpha[2] - alpha[1] effe3 = alpha[3] - alpha[1] effe4 = alpha[4] - alpha[1] effe5 = alpha[5] - alpha[1] test1 = (effe2 + effe3) - (effe4 + effe5) test2 = effe5 - 2 * effe4 return (; effe2, effe3, effe4, effe5, test1, test2) end model = fixed_effects(y, pop, nPops) chain = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, 4; progress=false) ``` ::: ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using FlexiChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools summarystats(chain) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: And check trace plots. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using StatsPlots plot(chain) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### 7.2.6 DIY Maximum Likelihood Estimates There are a couple of differences to keep in mind in using Julia rather than R. * Matrix Multiplication: In R, you would use `%*%` to multiply $X$ and α. In Julia, the standard `*` operator performs true matrix multiplication automatically when the left operand is a Matrix and the right is a Vector. * Preventing Domain Errors: The line `if σ <= 0.0 return Inf end` is a critical Julia optimization pattern. Unlike R's `optim()` which can sometimes suppress internal warnings, Distributions.jl will throw a hard error if you try to instantiate a Normal distribution with a negative standard deviation. Returning Inf cleanly tells Optim.jl to move away from that parameter space. * Anonymous Functions for Optimizers: R's optim allows you to pass additional data arguments (like y and X) via the ... argument. Optim.jl strictly expects a function of a single variable (the parameter vector). The syntax `p -> NLL(p, y, X)` creates a fast, on-the-fly closure that satisfies this requirement. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Distributions using Optim using Statistics # Define the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) function function NLL(param, y, X) α = param[1:5] σ = param[6] # The optimizer will sometimes test negative values for sigma. # Returning Inf acts as a hard boundary to prevent domain errors. if σ <= 0.0 return Inf end # Matrix multiplication: X (n x 5) * alpha (5 x 1) = mu (n x 1) μ = X * α # Calculate the negative sum of the log-likelihoods return -sum(logpdf.(Normal.(μ, σ), y)) end # Build the design matrix (X) # This creates an n x 5 matrix of zeros, then places a 1.0 in the column # corresponding to the population index for each observation. n = length(y) X = zeros(Float64, n, 5) for i in 1:n X[i, pop[i]] = 1.0 end # Set initial values for the optimizer # A good starting point is the global mean of y for the alphas, and the global standard deviation for sigma init_param = [fill(mean(y), 5); std(y)] # Run the optimizer # We use an anonymous function (p -> NLL(p, y, X)) to pass the data along with the parameters result = optimize(p -> NLL(p, y, X), init_param, NelderMead()) # Extract the MLE estimates mle_estimates = Optim.minimizer(result) round.(mle_estimates, digits=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6-element Vector{Float64}: 52.473 39.305 47.033 50.611 62.257 4.076 ``` ::: ::: ## 7.3 Random Effects The main point of this chapter is highlighting the difference between fixed effects and random effects models in the context of hierarchical data. So let's get into it. * Fixed effects (β parameters): These are the parameters we treat as constant across the population (or the specific contrasts we care about). We put priors directly on them. They represent the "average" or "overall" effect (e.g., global intercept, slope of a covariate like year or habitat). * Random effects (u or α parameters): These are group-specific deviations (e.g., site-specific intercepts, year-specific intercepts). We model them as coming from a common probability distribution (usually Normal(0, σ_group)), with hyperparameters (mean μ_group, usually 0 after centering, and variance σ_group²) that are themselves estimated. This induces partial pooling / shrinkage. This is the key Bayesian hierarchical insight: random effects are parameters with their own priors that are estimated from the data, allowing us to borrow strength across groups while quantifying group-level variation. Random effects 'soak up' variance that would otherwise inflate the residual error, leading to more accurate estimates of both group-level and overall effects. Fixed effects, on the other hand, are treated as constant across groups and capture the overall mean trends in the data. In code, we can see the difference in the parameters. Fixed effects will be coded like `β ~ Normal(0, 10)` while random effects will be coded like `α[group] ~ Normal(0, σ_group)`, with a hyperprior on the group-level standard deviation, e.g., `σ_group ~ Exponential(1)`. The parameters of the distribution are not fixed quantities, they are defined on a separate line of code and shared. ### 7.3.1 Data generation In Julia we would create the data as follows. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Distributions, CategoricalArrays nPops = 10 nSample = 12 n = nPops * nSample pop_grand_mean = 50 pop_sd = 3 pop_means = rand(Normal(pop_grand_mean, pop_sd), nPops) σ = 5 ε = rand(Normal(0, σ), n) pop = repeat(1:nPops, inner=nSample) pop = CategoricalArray(pop) Xmat = hcat([pop .== i for i in 1:nPops]...) y = Xmat * pop_means + ε ``` ::: The R code to generate the data is: ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} R""" set.seed(73) nPops <- 10 nSample <- 12 n <- nPops * nSample pop.grand.mean <- 50 pop.sd <- 3 pop.means <- rnorm(n=nPops, mean=pop.grand.mean, sd=pop.sd) sigma <- 5 eps <- rnorm(n=n, mean=0, sd=sigma) pop <- factor(rep(1:nPops, rep(nSample, nPops))) Xmat <- as.matrix(model.matrix(~ pop -1)) y <- as.numeric(Xmat %*% as.matrix(pop.means) + eps) """ @rget y ``` ::: ### 7.3.2 Likelihood analysis with canned functions The julia equivalent of lme4 is MixedModels.jl. See for a comparison with R. ::: {#mixed-model-fit .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using MixedModels, DataFrames df = DataFrame(y=y, pop=pop) form = @formula(y ~ 1 + (1 | pop)) model = fit(MixedModel,form, df) print(model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood y ~ 1 + (1 | pop) logLik -2 logLik AIC AICc BIC -377.4275 754.8551 760.8551 761.0620 769.2176 Variance components: Column Variance Std.Dev. pop (Intercept) 7.17234 2.67812 Residual 28.09962 5.30091 Number of obs: 120; levels of grouping factors: 10 Fixed-effects parameters: ───────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef.
